title: Operator Score Matching for Learning Quantum Hamiltonians
authors: Shreya Shukla, Abhijith Jayakumar, Andrey Y. Lokhov
abstract: Learning quantum Hamiltonians from low-temperature thermal state measurements is a fundamental problem in quantum physics. Scalability of existing methods is limited by the complexity of semidefinite optimization problems or partition function computation. Here, we develop a quantum analog of classical score matching method that exploits generalized notions of derivatives and integration by parts in operator algebras. We introduce a new \emph{Operator Score Matching} loss function that recovers Hamiltonian parameters by a simple gradient descent without the need to compute intractable normalization constants. Numerical experiments on the Gibbs states of the transverse-field Ising model, XXZ spin chain, Fermi-Hubbard model, and lattice $φ^4$ theory demonstrate efficient parameter recovery using finite-depth truncations of nested commutator expansions. Our results establish Operator Score Matching as a practical, partition-function-free framework for quantum Hamiltonian learning.
summary: This paper introduces Operator Score Matching, a novel, partition-function-free technique to determine the Hamiltonian of a quantum system from its thermal state measurements. By adapting classical score matching to the language of operator algebras, it provides a robust and scalable framework for quantum Hamiltonian learning. This is particularly valuable for studying strongly correlated electron models where exact calculations are intractable.
main_problem: The core problem is learning the microscopic Hamiltonian (H) that governs a quantum system solely from measurements of its low-temperature thermal state ($ho \propto e^{-H}$).
main_result: The authors introduce Operator Score Matching, a partition-function-free framework that efficiently recovers Hamiltonian parameters using simple gradient descent.
method: They adapt classical score matching by developing a quantum analog using generalized derivatives and an integration-by-parts identity in operator algebras to construct a computable loss function.
model_or_system: The method is tested on various models, including the transverse-field Ising model, XXZ spin chain, Fermi-Hubbard model, and lattice $\phi^4$ theory, applicable to both spin and fermionic systems.
key_observables: The operator score loss function, $L_{	ext{osm}}(	heta)$, which measures the difference between predicted and target operator scores.
important_parameters: The inverse temperature ($ eta$) and the depth ($d$) of the nested commutator expansion used for approximation are key parameters.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of direction operators $\{F_k\}$ that generate the full algebra for unique Hamiltonian determination, and convergence relies on establishing a local Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the fundamental problem of Hamiltonian learning, develops the Operator Score Matching loss function using algebraic identities, demonstrates its applicability across multiple physical models (Ising, Fermi-Hubbard), and concludes with convergence guarantees via the PL inequality.
why_interesting: This provides a powerful, computationally tractable alternative to traditional methods (like those relying on partition function calculations) for characterizing complex many-body Hamiltonians from limited experimental data.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic of quantum score matching through local probes Fk. Left: A local kick generated by an operator Fk perturbs the Gibbs state ρ, producing a score response DkH′ that spreads around the lattice site with truncation depth d. Middle: Learning is performed by comparing the response fingerprints of the target Hamiltonian H′ and the model Hamiltonian Hθ under the same probes Fk and minimizing the discrepancy. Right: Identifiability is controlled by probe coverage: when the set {Fk} probes all nontrivial directions in the model class span{hi}, no hidden Hamiltonian direction remains invisible, and matching all responses determines Hθ up to an additive constant.

FIG. 2: Loss landscape for a single qubit with H = a σz + b σx. Top: Contour plot of the loss L(a, b). Bottom: Contour plot of the norm squared of the gradient, |∇L(a, b)|2. As is evident, this loss has a unique minimum at the true couplings (a∗, b∗) = (1.0, 0.5).
